clause_evidence.clause: Illustrate and apply properties of multiplication
clause_evidence.reasoning: All thirty samples require students to identify and apply one of the five named properties through comparison items, error detection tasks, or direct calculation; students must both understand each property and determine whether specific expressions correctly demonstrate it.

Every sample includes at least one factor from the specified set of 6, 7, 8, or 9; under ruling 18, facts belong to the table of any factor that names that table number, so expressions like five times six are valid facts of the six table.

clause_evidence.clause: one multiplied by any number is equal to the number
clause_evidence.reasoning: Six samples explicitly test the identity property with one as a factor; students encounter one times various numbers from the specified tables and must recognize that the product always equals the other factor, whether in direct calculation or true-false evaluation.

clause_evidence.clause: zero multiplied by any number is zero
clause_evidence.reasoning: Three samples test the zero property through direct multiplication tasks and error detection; students must identify that zero times any number from the specified tables always produces zero and recognize when this property is misapplied.

clause_evidence.clause: changing the order of the numbers being multiplied does not change the product
clause_evidence.reasoning: Eight samples test the commutative property by presenting multiplication expressions with factors in different orders and asking whether they are equivalent; students must apply the principle that reordering factors does not affect the product of two numbers from the specified tables.

clause_evidence.clause: changing the grouping of the numbers being multiplied does not change the product
clause_evidence.reasoning: Six samples test the associative property using three factors with different parenthetical groupings; students must determine whether changing how factors are grouped affects the final product and recognize both cases where grouping changes preserve the product and cases where different factors produce different results.

clause_evidence.clause: multiplying the sum of two addends by a number is the same as the sum of the products of a number by each addend
clause_evidence.reasoning: Five samples test the distributive property by comparing multiplying a sum against distributing the multiplication across individual addends; students encounter both correct applications where the results are equivalent and incorrect applications where only one addend receives multiplication, requiring them to apply the property accurately.
